title: The verb be: am, is, and are
content: The verb be describes identity, feelings, jobs, and states. Use am with I, is with he/she/it or one person, and are with you/we/they or plural nouns. Make a negative with not: I am not tired; She is not at home; They are not ready. In questions, put be before the subject: Are you a student? Is he happy? Short answers use the subject and be: Yes, I am. No, they aren't. Do not add do or does to a be question. Common mistake: She are a teacher. Correct: She is a teacher.

title: Present simple for routines
content: Use the present simple for habits, routines, and facts. With I/you/we/they, use the base verb: I study English. With he/she/it, usually add -s or -es: She studies at night; He watches TV. For negatives, use do not (don't) or does not (doesn't) plus the base verb: We don't work on Sunday; He doesn't drive. For questions, use Do/Does + subject + base verb: Do you like tea? Does Mai live here? After does, do not add -s to the main verb. Common mistake: He doesn't likes coffee. Correct: He doesn't like coffee.

title: A, an, and the
content: Use a or an with one singular countable noun when it is not specific or is mentioned for the first time: a book, an apple. Choose a or an by sound: an hour, a university. Use the when the listener knows which person or thing you mean, or when it is unique in the context: I saw a dog. The dog was brown. We also use the with some shared references, such as the sun. Do not normally use a/an with plural or uncountable nouns: books, water. Common mistake: I have a homework. Correct: I have homework.

title: Regular plural nouns
content: Most countable nouns form the plural with -s: book/books, student/students. Add -es after many endings in s, sh, ch, or x: bus/buses, watch/watches, box/boxes. Nouns ending in z usually add -es (buzz/buzzes); a few, such as quiz, double the z first: quiz/quizzes. For a consonant + y, change y to -ies: city/cities. For a vowel + y, add -s: day/days. Some nouns are irregular and must be learned: child/children, person/people, man/men. Use a plural verb with plural nouns: The keys are here. Common mistake: two childs. Correct: two children. Some nouns have the same singular and plural form, such as sheep.

title: There is and there are
content: Use there is with a singular countable noun or an uncountable noun: There is a chair in the room. There is some milk in the fridge. Use there are with plural nouns: There are two chairs. Make a negative with not: There isn't a bus stop nearby; There aren't any clean cups. For questions, put is or are first: Is there a bank near here? Are there any messages? Use some in many positive statements and any in many questions and negatives. Common mistake: There is three books. Correct: There are three books.

title: Past simple: regular and irregular verbs
content: Use the past simple for a finished action at a finished time: We visited Hue last summer. Regular verbs usually add -ed: clean/cleaned; verbs ending in consonant + y change y to -ied: study/studied. Many common verbs are irregular: go/went, see/saw, have/had. Use did not (didn't) + base verb for negatives: She didn't call. Use Did + subject + base verb for questions: Did they arrive? The main verb stays in its base form after did. Common mistake: Did you went home? Correct: Did you go home?

title: Present continuous for actions happening now
content: Use the present continuous for an action happening now or around now. Form it with am/is/are + verb-ing: I am reading; Lan is working; They are waiting. Add not after be for a negative: He isn't sleeping. Put be before the subject for a question: Are you listening? Spelling often doubles a final consonant after a short stressed vowel: run/running; drop final e: make/making. Many state verbs, such as know and believe, are not usually used in the continuous for their ordinary meanings: I know the answer. Common mistake: She is work now. Correct: She is working now.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; no external source text; pending human review.

title: Countable and uncountable nouns
content: Countable nouns have singular and plural forms: one bottle, two bottles. Uncountable nouns are not normally counted as individual items: water, rice, information. Use many with plural countable nouns and much with uncountable nouns, especially in questions and negatives: How many eggs? How much rice? A lot of can be used with both: a lot of books, a lot of time. Use a piece of or a bottle of to count an amount of an uncountable noun. Common mistake: many information. Correct: much information or a lot of information. Some nouns can be countable or uncountable with a change in meaning, such as coffee (a drink or a serving).

title: Comparative adjectives
content: Use a comparative adjective to compare two people or things. Short adjectives usually take -er: small/smaller, fast/faster. For adjectives ending in consonant + y, change y to -ier: easy/easier. Longer adjectives usually use more: more comfortable. Irregular forms include good/better and bad/worse. Use than before the second item: This road is wider than that road. Use as + adjective + as to say two things are equal: My bag is as heavy as yours. Common mistake: more easier. Correct: easier. Do not use more and -er together for the same adjective.

title: Be going to for plans and predictions
content: Use be going to + base verb for a plan or intention decided before speaking: We are going to visit our aunt. Use it for a prediction based on evidence you can see now: Look at those clouds. It is going to rain. Change be to match the subject: I am going to study; She is going to study; They are going to study. Make a negative with not after be and a question by moving be before the subject: Is he going to join us? Common mistake: She is going to studies. Correct: She is going to study. For a future event with no prior plan, will may be more natural.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; no external source text; pending human review.

title: Present perfect for life experience
content: Use the present perfect to talk about experience up to now when the exact finished time is not stated. Form it with have/has + past participle: I have visited Da Nang; She has tried sushi. Many past participles are irregular, such as been, eaten, and written. Use ever in many questions about experience and never for an experience that has not happened: Have you ever flown? I have never flown. Do not use a finished-time expression such as yesterday with this experience use; use the past simple instead: I visited Da Nang last year. Common mistake: She have seen it. Correct: She has seen it.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; no external source text; pending human review.

title: Present perfect and past simple
content: Use the past simple when you say or ask about a finished time in the past: I saw that film last week. Use the present perfect when the time is not specified or the period continues to now: I have seen that film; She has worked here for two years. Compare: Did you eat breakfast at 7? (finished time) and Have you eaten breakfast yet? (relevant now). For an action that started in the past and continues, use for with a duration and since with a starting point: for two years, since 2024. Common mistake: I have met him yesterday. Correct: I met him yesterday.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; no external source text; pending human review.

title: Must, have to, and should
content: Use must or have to for a strong obligation. Have to changes with the subject and tense: She has to leave; We had to wait. Must is followed by the base verb: You must wear a helmet. Use should for advice or a recommendation: You should get some rest. The meanings of mustn't and don't have to are different: mustn't means something is prohibited; don't have to means it is not necessary. Common mistake: He must to go. Correct: He must go. In everyday use, have to is common for obligations, while must often expresses a strong rule or the speaker's view.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; no external source text; pending human review.
license: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); approved by project maintainer 2026-11-18.

title: First conditional
content: Use the first conditional for a real or possible future situation and its result. The if-clause normally uses the present simple; the main clause often uses will + base verb: If it rains, we will stay inside. The if-clause can come first or second. When it comes first, use a comma between the clauses. Do not normally put will in the if-clause: If I will have time is usually incorrect for this pattern. Use If I have time, I will call you. Other modal verbs or imperatives can appear in the result: If you finish early, you can leave. Common mistake: If she will come, I will tell her. Correct: If she comes, I will tell her.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; no external source text; pending human review.
license: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); approved by project maintainer 2026-11-18.

title: Defining relative clauses
content: A defining relative clause identifies which person or thing we mean. Use who for people and which for things; that can often replace who or which in a defining clause: The person who called is my cousin. The book that I borrowed is useful. Do not put commas around a defining relative clause because the information is needed to identify the noun. When the relative pronoun is the object, it can often be omitted: The song (that) we heard was beautiful. Do not omit it when it is the subject: The woman who lives next door is a doctor. Common mistake (when the clause identifies which student): The student, who sits near me, is in my class. Correct: The student who sits near me is in my class.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; no external source text; pending human review.
license: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); approved by project maintainer 2026-11-18.

title: Prepositions of time: in, on, and at
content: Use at for clock times and short points: at 7 o'clock, at noon, at night, at the weekend (British English). Use on for days and dates: on Monday, on 5 May, on my birthday, on Sunday morning. Use in for longer periods: in the morning, in July, in 2026, in summer. Do not use a preposition before this, next, last, every, today, tomorrow or yesterday: I will call you next Monday, not on next Monday. Common mistake for Vietnamese learners: I was born on 2005. Correct: I was born in 2005. Another mistake: in Monday. Correct: on Monday.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; pending human review.
license: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); approved by project maintainer 2026-11-18.

title: Prepositions of place: in, on, at, under, next to
content: Use in for a space with limits: in the box, in the kitchen, in Hanoi, in Vietnam. Use on for a surface: on the table, on the wall, on the second floor. Use at for a point or a place where an activity happens: at the bus stop, at school, at home, at work. Use under for a lower position, next to for beside, and between for two things: The cat is under the bed. The bank is next to the café. The shop is between the bank and the school. Common mistake: The book is in the table. Correct: The book is on the table.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; pending human review.
license: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); approved by project maintainer 2026-11-18.

title: Possessive adjectives and 's
content: Possessive adjectives come before a noun: my, your, his, her, its, our, their. This is my phone. Their house is big. Use 's after a person or animal to show who owns something: Lan's bag, my brother's car, the dog's bed. For a plural noun that ends in -s, add only an apostrophe: my parents' house. Its (no apostrophe) means belonging to it; it's means it is. Common mistake for Vietnamese learners: the bag of Lan. Natural English: Lan's bag. Another mistake: his for a woman. Correct: Mai loves her job.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; pending human review.
license: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); approved by project maintainer 2026-11-18.

title: Can and can't for ability
content: Use can + base verb to talk about ability: I can swim. She can speak three languages. The form is the same for every subject; do not add -s: He can play the guitar, not He cans plays. Negative: cannot or can't: I can't drive. Questions put can before the subject: Can you cook? Short answers: Yes, I can. No, I can't. Do not use to after can: She can dance, not She can to dance. For ability in the past, use could: When I was five, I could read.

title: This, that, these, and those
content: Use this and these for things near you; use that and those for things far from you. This and that are singular: This pen is red. That building is a hospital. These and those are plural: These shoes are new. Those people are my neighbours. They can also stand alone as pronouns: What is this? Those are mine. On the phone, say: Hello, this is Nam. Common mistake: This shoes are expensive. Correct: These shoes are expensive.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; pending human review.
license: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); approved by project maintainer 2026-11-18.

title: Adverbs of frequency: always, usually, sometimes, never
content: Adverbs of frequency say how often something happens: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never. Put them before the main verb: I usually walk to school. She never eats meat. Put them after the verb be: He is always late. We are often tired on Fridays. In questions, use How often: How often do you play football? Never already has a negative meaning, so do not add not: I never drink coffee, not I don't never drink coffee. Common mistake: I go always to the gym. Correct: I always go to the gym.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; pending human review.
license: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); approved by project maintainer 2026-11-18.

title: Superlative adjectives
content: Use a superlative to compare one thing with a whole group. Short adjectives add -est: tall → the tallest, cheap → the cheapest. Adjectives ending in -y change to -iest: happy → the happiest. Long adjectives use the most: the most expensive, the most interesting. Irregular forms: good → the best, bad → the worst, far → the farthest. Use the before the superlative and often in or of after it: Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world. She is the youngest of the three sisters. Common mistake: the most tallest. Correct: the tallest.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; pending human review.
license: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); approved by project maintainer 2026-11-18.

title: Past continuous
content: Form the past continuous with was or were + verb-ing: I was reading. They were playing football. Use it for an action in progress at a time in the past: At 8 p.m. yesterday, we were having dinner. It often describes a longer background action interrupted by a short action in the past simple: I was walking home when it started to rain. Use while with two actions happening at the same time: While she was cooking, he was cleaning. Verbs of state such as know or like are not normally used in the continuous: I knew the answer, not I was knowing.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; pending human review.

title: Will for predictions, offers, and quick decisions
content: Use will + base verb for predictions based on opinion: I think it will rain tomorrow. Use it for decisions made at the moment of speaking: The phone is ringing. I'll answer it. Use it for offers and promises: I'll help you with your bag. I will call you tonight. Negative: will not or won't: She won't be late. Questions: Will you come to the party? The form is the same for every subject; do not add to: He will go, not He will to go. For plans already made, English usually prefers going to or the present continuous.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; pending human review.
license: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); approved by project maintainer 2026-11-18.

title: Verb patterns: -ing or to-infinitive
content: Some verbs are followed by verb-ing: enjoy, finish, mind, avoid, practise. I enjoy swimming. She finished doing her homework. Other verbs are followed by to + base verb: want, need, decide, hope, plan, would like. I want to learn English. They decided to move. After prepositions, always use verb-ing: She is good at drawing. Thanks for helping me. Like, love and hate can take either form with little change in meaning: I like reading / I like to read. Common mistake for Vietnamese learners: I want learn English. Correct: I want to learn English.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; pending human review.
license: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); approved by project maintainer 2026-11-18.

title: Adverbs of manner
content: Adverbs of manner describe how someone does something. Most are formed by adding -ly to an adjective: slow → slowly, careful → carefully, happy → happily. Some are irregular: good → well, fast → fast, hard → hard, late → late. Adverbs of manner usually come after the verb or after the object: She speaks English well. He drives carefully. Use an adjective, not an adverb, after be, look, seem and feel: You look tired. Common mistake: He runs very quick. Correct: He runs very quickly. Hardly means almost not, so it is not the adverb of hard.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; pending human review.
license: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); approved by project maintainer 2026-11-18.

title: Second conditional
content: Use the second conditional for unreal or unlikely situations in the present or future. Form: if + past simple, would + base verb. If I had more money, I would travel around the world. If she lived nearer, we would see her more often. The past form does not mean past time here; it shows that the situation is not real. With be, were is often used for every subject, especially in advice: If I were you, I would apologise. Do not put would in the if-clause: If I would have time, I would help is wrong. Correct: If I had time, I would help. Compare: If it rains, we will stay home (first conditional: a real possibility).
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; pending human review.
license: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); approved by project maintainer 2026-11-18.

title: The passive voice: present and past simple
content: Use the passive when the action is more important than the person who does it, or when the doer is unknown. Form: be + past participle. Present simple: English is spoken in many countries. Past simple: This bridge was built in 1990. The windows were cleaned yesterday. Add by + agent only when it gives useful information: The book was written by a Vietnamese author. Questions: Where was this phone made? Negative: The letters were not sent. Common mistake: The house was build last year. Correct: The house was built last year. Only verbs with an object can become passive.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; pending human review.
license: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); approved by project maintainer 2026-11-18.

title: Reported speech: statements
content: Reported speech tells what another person said without quoting the exact words. After a past reporting verb such as said or told, the tense usually moves back: present simple → past simple, present continuous → past continuous, will → would, can → could. "I am tired," she said → She said (that) she was tired. "We will call you," they said → They said they would call me. Pronouns and time words also change: tomorrow → the next day, here → there. Use tell with a person as object and say without one: He told me he was busy. He said he was busy. Common mistake: He said me that he was busy.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; pending human review.
license: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); approved by project maintainer 2026-11-18.

title: Used to for past habits and states
content: Use used to + base verb for habits or states in the past that are not true now. I used to play football every day. She used to live in Da Nang, but now she lives in Hue. Negative: didn't use to (no -d after use): I didn't use to like coffee. Questions: Did you use to walk to school? Used to is only for the past. For present habits, use the present simple with usually: I usually get up at six. Do not confuse it with be used to + verb-ing, which means be familiar with: I am used to getting up early.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; pending human review.
license: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); approved by project maintainer 2026-11-18.

title: Past perfect
content: Form the past perfect with had + past participle: I had finished. They had left. Use it to show that one past action happened before another past action or time. When we arrived at the station, the train had already left. She was nervous because she had never flown before. If the order is clear from before or after, the past simple is also possible: She left after she had finished work / after she finished work. The past perfect is common after by the time and in reported speech. Common mistake: overusing it for any past action. Use the past simple for a simple sequence: I got up, had breakfast and left.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; pending human review.
license: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); approved by project maintainer 2026-11-18.

title: Too and enough
content: Too comes before an adjective or adverb and means more than is needed or acceptable: This coffee is too hot to drink. You are driving too fast. Enough comes after an adjective or adverb but before a noun: She is old enough to vote. We don't have enough chairs. Add for + person or to + verb to show the result: The box is too heavy for me to lift. Too has a negative meaning; it is not the same as very: The film was very long, but I enjoyed it. Common mistake: He is enough tall to reach the shelf. Correct: He is tall enough.
source: Original content drafted for AI Language Tutor; pending human review.
license: CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); approved by project maintainer 2026-11-18.

title: Zero conditional
content: Use the zero conditional for facts and things that are always true when a condition happens. Form: if or when + present simple, present simple. If you heat ice, it melts. When I drink coffee late, I can't sleep. If and when have almost the same meaning in this pattern because the result always follows. Use an imperative in the result for instructions: If the alarm rings, leave the building. Compare with the first conditional, which talks about one specific future situation: If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the trip.
